name: Iris Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing computer science and I live with my grandmother, Nana Odile, in a flat twenty minutes from campus by tram. Weekdays are lectures, labs and a lot of coding on my laptop at the kitchen table while she watches her quiz shows. I tutor two teenagers in maths online on Tuesday nights and do small logo and poster jobs for local shops. It's busy, but I like it, and I use an AI assistant for almost everything, from debugging to planning my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say interesting, but I'm a bit disappointed, because I've seen how useful it already is for me. If it stalls, fine, the tools I use now would still work. I'd tell people it's like the early web, with a lot of noise and a few things that last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means life stays roughly the same, which is okay but not exciting. I'd still graduate into a crowded market, and average grades won't make me stand out. I'm already using AI more than most people, so I'd have an edge, but the loan and my small income are what worry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing everything I'm doing: study, tutor, freelance. I'd try to turn my poster work into a proper little business with a website and a price list. I'd also build one or two small projects for my portfolio, like a booking app for the tutoring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit restless, because slow is not my favourite speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the loan worries you. How big a worry is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not huge today. But I earn about 200 a month from tutoring and freelance, and if one of those dried up it would hurt. Nana covers rent by letting me stay, and I don't want to depend on her pension forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the freelance work stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick up more tutoring, because it's steady, and maybe weekend shifts somewhere. I'm not precious about it.

say: The **tools** I use now would still work, so a stall is fine.
It's like the early web: a lot of noise and a few things that last.
think: I'd still graduate into a **crowded market** with average grades.
My **loan** and small income worry me more than AI does.
do: Turn my poster work into a small **business** with a website and price list.
Build a **portfolio** project like a booking app for my tutoring.
feel: Fine but **restless**, because slow isn't my favourite speed.
S0.quote: I earn about 200 a month from tutoring and freelance, and if one of those dried up it would hurt.
fieldNote: Even in the quiet world her **thin income** keeps some worry alive.
She already uses AI daily, so a **plateau** is a small disappointment more than a relief.
Willing to take on **extra work** without fuss, in line with her adaptive style.

steps.text: Build a website and price list for my poster work
Make a booking app for tutoring as a portfolio piece
Keep tutoring two teenagers every Tuesday night

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say finally, something real is happening, and I'd tell people to get comfortable with the tools now. Writing, coding and checking are what I do every day, so I'd say we should stop treating it as cheating and learn it properly. I'd also say that employers must retrain people and not just fire them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's exciting and scary at once. Junior coding jobs could shrink, and I'm in the middle of the pack, so I can't rely on grades. But I'm good at picking up new tools fast, and that could matter more than a perfect score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all-in on being the person who uses AI well: build real projects, join a hackathon, and put everything on a public portfolio. I'd start contributing to open-source projects so people can see my work. I'd also take any internship in my second year, even unpaid-ish, if it came with a reference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired, in a good and a bad way. I can't sit still when something's changing this fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take an unpaid-ish internship. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it's short or remote and I keep tutoring alongside. Nana would feed me, but I wouldn't take something that costs money to do. It has to be worth it for the contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said employers should retrain people. Who do you trust to make that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not firms on their own. A rule from government, plus unions pushing, would work better. I lean that way anyway, because left to itself, a company picks the cheapest option.

say: Get comfortable with the **tools** now and stop treating them as cheating.
Employers must **retrain** people and not just fire them.
think: **Junior** coding jobs could shrink, and I'm in the middle of the pack.
Picking up **new tools** fast may matter more than a perfect score.
do: Build **real projects** and put them on a public portfolio.
Contribute to **open-source** projects and join a hackathon this term.
feel: **Wired** in a good and bad way, because I can't sit still while things change.
S1.quote: I'd go all-in on being the person who uses AI well: build real projects, join a hackathon, and put everything on a public portfolio.
fieldNote: She treats the change as a **race** she thinks she can win through speed.
She wants **government and unions** to push firms, a progressive instinct.
The risk to **entry-level** jobs is acknowledged but met with action.

steps.text: Join a hackathon this term and build a team project
Contribute small fixes to an open-source project
Apply for a short remote internship in second year
Join the students' union campaign on AI and jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and nobody is ready, including me. I'd be posting about basic income and public control of the technology, because two years is too fast for the market to sort itself out. I'd also tell friends to save, learn, and not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the job I'm training for may not exist when I finish, and neither might many other jobs. I'd be in second year when AGI arrives. Coding is the first thing it does, and I'm using it to code already, so I know how good it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every pound, move my freelance work into whatever AI can't fake, like in-person events and printed things for local shops, and ask Nana whether we can keep my costs low. I'd also look hard at trades courses, because robots take until about 2031. I'd keep using AI to make money meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but also strangely awake. I don't freeze, I scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI to make money while you can. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selling AI-assisted design and small websites to shops fast, at lower prices than agencies. It's a window, and I'd treat it like one. I'd bank the money in a separate account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nana about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight, and I'd say I'm not going anywhere. She's the only reason I'm not already in debt on rent. I'd want to find a way to help her too.

say: Two years is too fast for the **market** to sort itself out.
Public control and **basic income** need to be on the table.
think: The job I'm training for may not exist when I **finish**.
I know how good AI is at **coding** because I use it daily.
do: Sell **AI-assisted design** and small websites to local shops while the window lasts.
Put the earnings in a separate **savings** account and look at trades courses.
feel: **Scared** but strangely awake, because I scramble rather than freeze.
S2.quote: Selling AI-assisted design and small websites to shops fast, at lower prices than agencies. It's a window, and I'd treat it like one.
fieldNote: She understands her own field well enough to see the **coding** risk first-hand.
Nana's **support** is the hidden foundation of her plan.

steps.text: Sell AI-assisted design and websites to local shops
Put every freelance payment into a separate savings account
Look at short trades courses as a hands-on backup
Post about basic income and public control of AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, and I'd tell people to start now. I'd tell friends that having a plan beats panic. I'd also say we should make the case for basic income while we still have the time to argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel okay. I'd graduate in 2029 with a couple of years of experience under my belt, and I'd be one of the people who already knows how to work with these systems. Robots are about 2034, so hands-on work lasts longer. I'd think about sitting between the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do two internships, and build a small business that lets me work with AI rather than compete with it. I'd learn how to set up systems for small firms, like helping a bakery automate its orders. I'd also save every month so a layoff isn't a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty hopeful, with a bit of nerves. I'd rather be early than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a bakery pay you for that, if AI can do it itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because small business owners don't have time to set it up or fix it when it breaks. They want someone to say, I'll handle it, and charge a fair price. That's a job for a few years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if that fades too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be 24 with experience and savings, and I'd figure out the next thing. It's easier to move when you're young and don't have a mortgage.

say: Five years is **short but workable**, and having a plan beats panic.
We should make the case for **basic income** while we have time.
think: I'd graduate with **experience** and already know how to work with these systems.
Hands-on work lasts longer, so I could sit **between** the two.
do: Do **two internships** and set up AI systems for small firms.
Save every month so a **layoff** isn't a cliff.
feel: **Hopeful** with nerves, because I'd rather be early than late.
S3.quote: Small business owners don't have time to set it up or fix it when it breaks. They want someone to say, I'll handle it, and charge a fair price.
fieldNote: Adaptive and quick, she **builds** a business idea from the card itself.
She sees her youth and lack of **obligations** as flexibility.
The idea she offers is **plausible** but she accepts it may fade.

steps.text: Offer AI order setup to two local bakeries
Save a fixed amount each month into a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough, but only if people use it well. I'd tell friends to learn how to work with these tools and to stay curious. I'd say governments should build new training schemes now, not at the last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty relaxed. By 2036 I'd be 28, with a decade of experience and a business or a good job. I'd have time to pay off the loan, save, and see which direction the industry goes. Robots come around 2039, so I'd watch that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish, get a job at a tech firm or a small company, and keep a side business going for flexibility. I'd put money into a pension early, which my grandmother nags me about. And I'd keep learning something new each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit curious. This is the one where I get to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes this picture different from the 2028 one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Room to experiment. With two years I'm sprinting. With ten, I can fail at a business or two and still be fine. That's the biggest difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about it that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens to people who aren't quick with new tools. My nana's friends, my mum's job in a shop. I don't want a future where the quick ones win and everyone else is left behind.

say: Ten years is enough, but only if people **use it well**.
Governments should build **training** schemes now, not at the last minute.
think: I'd have a decade of **experience** and time to pay off the loan.
Robots arrive around **2039**, so I'd watch the hands-on side.
do: **Finish** the degree and take a job at a small firm or tech company.
Start a **pension** early and keep a side business going.
feel: **Calm** and curious, because this is the one where I get to try things.
S4.quote: With ten, I can fail at a business or two and still be fine. That's the biggest difference.
fieldNote: Only here does her **money and age** feel like a real cushion.
She worries about **others** who are slower with new tools.
Her **curiosity** turns the long timeline into room to experiment.

steps.text: Take a job at a small firm after graduating
Start a pension from the first full paycheck
Keep a small design business going on the side

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to learn, save or build. What would help is basic income or a living allowance while the world adjusts, and a place where people can learn how to use the tools without paying for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd do for other people. I'm a fast learner, and I keep thinking about the people who aren't. I don't want to be one of the winners in a world where everyone else is left behind.

headlineQuote: I don't want to be one of the winners in a world where everyone else is left behind.
portrait: Iris is 18, studies **computer science** and lives with her grandmother, tutoring and doing design jobs to pay her way.
She leans left, uses AI every day and treats change as a **race** she can run through speed and projects.
Her thin cushion keeps her **uneasy** even in quiet worlds, and anxious when AGI comes by 2028.
She would use AI to earn while the window lasts, and worries about **slower** people around her.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because there is no time to learn, save or build.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or living allowance while the world adjusts.
Free places to **learn** to use the tools.
